newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Russia extradites Azeri ex-premier to Azerbaijan. [CORRECTED 01:28 GMT 28/3]
newsitem.headline: Russia extradites Azeri ex-premier to Azerbaijan. [CORRECTED 01:28 GMT 28/3]

text.p: Former Azeri prime minister Suret Guseynov, extradited from Russia after a long campaign by Baku, arrived here on Thursday to face charges of treason and armed rebellion and a possible death penalty.

Security officials said Guseynov, the most wanted man in Azerbaijan for allegedly plotting an attempted coup against President Haydar Aliyev in 1994, arrived in handcuffs on a scheduled plane from Moscow at 5 a.m. (0100 GMT).
They added that he was arrested near the central Russian town of Tula on March 20.

Azeri officials also accuse Guseynov, 39, appointed premier by Aliyev in July 1993, of involvement in an attempted coup in 1995 and of trying to organise a 1996 attempt on the life of the 73-year old leader, in which a group of assailants allegedly planned to shoot down his presidential plane.

The Azeri government had been seeking Guseynov's extradition for more than two years and his continued presence in Russia was a major stumbling block to improving generally poor ties between the two countries since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Political analysts said the timing of the extradition was significant, showing that Moscow wanted to improve relations before Friday's summit of the leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States, a loose union of 12 former Soviet republics.
The shadowy, slender Guseynov reportedly became a millionaire under communism in the 1980's when he ran a wool-processing plant in the central Azeri town of Yevlax.
He parlayed his economic clout into political power, commanding a private militia which helped overthrow democratically elected president Abulfaz Elchibey in 1993.
Guseynov's photograph graces most-wanted lists across the former Soviet republic and Baku has been pressing Moscow to find and extradite him.

Azeri officials say Moscow abetted Guseynov in his attempts to overthrow Aliyev, because it saw him as too pro-Western and unwilling to give Russia more of a role in lucrative offshore Caspian Sea oil projects.
Russia has always strenously denied the charges.

Azeri-Russian ties took a further blow earlier this month when Russian Defense Minister Igor Rodionov admitted that his country supplied large amounts of heavy weaponry to Azerbaijan's enemy and neighbor Armenia from 1994-96.

Moslem Azerbaijan and Christian Armenia have been in conflict for nine years over the disputed territory of Nagono-Karabakh, whose Armenian population have fought against rule by Baku. Azerbaijan has always alleged Russian covert support for Yerevan.
Fighting between Azeris and Armenians killed thousands before a cease-fire was agreed in 1994.

No lasting peace settlement has been found, (corrects from "now a lasting peace sttlement has been found") however and Armenia has offered to free Azeri prisoners taken in fighting over the Nagorno-Karabakh enclave as a unilateral gesture of goodwill ahead of talks in Moscow later this week.

Baku is still pressing Moscow to extradite former president Ayaz Mutalibov and others. Ousted in 1992, Mutalibov won support from the Russian parliament last year. Among other leaders who have been extradited by Russia, former defence minister Ragim Gaziyev was handed over last April.
